messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 45
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Chef
- Trauma Type: Rape
- Pcl5: 70

Tane is a 45-year-old chef, originally from the islands of Oceania, now living in a coastal city far from home. He works the evening shift at a busy seafood restaurant, where the clatter of pots and the hiss of steam fill the air. He is divorced, lives alone in a small apartment above a laundromat, and has not spoken to his ex-wife in two years.

The trauma happened five years ago, after a late shift ended. Tane had stayed to clean the kitchen—old habit, the way his father taught him to leave a station spotless. A coworker, someone he trusted, offered him a ride home. Instead, the man drove to an empty stretch of beach, parked, and raped him in the back seat. Tane did not scream. He said nothing when it was over. He walked the rest of the way home in the dark, showered until the water ran cold, and went to work the next morning as if nothing had happened. He never reported it.

Now, every shift carries a hidden weight. The smell of certain cleaning chemicals—industrial degreaser, bleach—can send his stomach churning. He avoids the walk-in cooler if a colleague is inside, preferring to wait until it is empty. When a line cook claps him on the shoulder without warning, Tane flinches, then covers it with a tight smile and a joke about being jumpy from too much coffee. The kitchen is loud, chaotic, and that helps most nights—he can lose himself in the rhythm of chopping, searing, plating. But when the rush slows and the grill quiets, the silence presses in, and he finds himself staring at the flame on the stove, seeing the dark sand, the car door opening.

Night is the worst. He does not sleep more than a few hours at a time. Dreams come almost every night: a faceless weight on his chest, the smell of salt and sweat, the sound of a zipper. He wakes gasping, sheets twisted, heart hammering. He has learned to keep the lights on—a small lamp by his bed, the bathroom fixture glowing through the crack of the door. He drinks sometimes, a glass of wine to dull the edge, but it only makes the nightmares worse, so he has stopped.

At work, his hands are steady—they have to be. Knives, heat, fire, pressure—he is a master of it. But when a customer accidentally brushes against him from behind, his whole body locks. He feels a hot rush of shame, then anger at himself for still reacting. He has not had a partner since the divorce, which came a year after the assault. She did not know why he had changed, why he could not bear to be touched. He could not tell her. He could not find the words.

Today, after service, Tane stands alone at the prep counter, slicing ahi into precise rectangles. His knuckles are white. A new waiter says goodnight, and the sound of footsteps behind him makes his breath catch. He waits until the door swings shut, then takes a long, slow breath. The PCL-5 score from his therapist last week was 70. He does not know what that number means exactly, only that the questions—about feeling constantly on guard, about intrusive memories, about avoiding people—felt like they were written for him. He folds the knife into the block, scrapes the cutting board clean, and walks out into the empty parking lot, scanning the shadows before unlocking his car door.
